references.text: Abraham asks his servant to swear that he will not take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites, but from his own family, which mirrors the instructions given to Jacob.
Rebekah is identified as the daughter of Bethuel from Paddan-Aram and sister to Laban the Aramean, the same lineage to which Jacob is now sent.
Esau takes Hittite wives, which was a source of grief for Isaac and Rebekah, underscoring the importance of choosing spouses from one's own family.
Rebekah expresses her frustration over Esau's Hittite wives and her fear that Jacob might do the same, which directly leads to Isaac's command in 28:1-2.
Jacob follows the instructions and travels to Paddan-Aram, where he arrives and meets Rachel at the well.
Hosea refers to Jacob's flight to the land of Aram and his service for a wife, reflecting Jacob's journey and mission in Paddan-Aram.
The repetition of the principle of taking a wife from the family in Aram emphasizes the continuity of God's plan for Abraham's descendants across generations.
Parallel between the generations: Abraham's son received a wife from the nearby region/Egypt, while Isaac sends Jacob far away to preserve the chosen line.
Direct narrative connection: 27:43 gives the reason for the journey (flight), while 28:2 specifies the purpose of the mission (marriage).
Theological contrast: Jacob's journey to Aram (28:2) is the starting point for the growth of the family, while Deut 26:5 refers to the later journey from Aram/Egypt that led to nation-building.
